Oil on canvas, 113 x 93 cm; National Gallery, London, inv. NG29 (https://www.wga.hu/html_m/b/barocci/gatto.html).

Around 35 preparatory drawings survive, including a full-size cartoon (private collection, France) (https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/federico-barocci-the-madonna-of-the-cat-la-madonna-del-gatto).

subject.reason: Confirmed by Wikipedia and the temple's official site: Gōtoku-ji is a real Sōtō Zen temple in Setagaya whose Shōfuku-den is surrounded by hundreds of white ceramic maneki-neko votive figurines.

source.reason: No museum catalogue exists for these votive objects; the temple's own official page is the institutional source, preferred over Wikipedia.

taxonomy.submovement: Edo-period Sōtō Zen temple votive ceramics
taxonomy.reason: Japanese Edo-origin temple craft; mov-japanese-ukiyo-e is the only Japanese movement in the taxonomy, and the submovement corrects the inaccurate 'Edo to Contemporary Buddhist Temple Votive Craft' label to a specific temple/craft tradition.

rights.reason: Anonymous, ongoing traditional craft with no single author or fixed publication date; individual figurines are contemporary, so public-domain status cannot be established.

facts: Gōtoku-ji was founded in 1480 and renamed in 1659 after Ii Naotaka, lord of Hikone, who rebuilt it in 1633 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C5%8Dtoku-ji).
The maneki-neko at Gōtoku-ji hold no coin (koban), symbolizing opportunity rather than direct monetary gain (https://gotokuji.jp/en/manekineko/).
The Shōfuku-den sanctuary enshrines the maneki-neko; devotees offer figurines after their wishes are fulfilled (https://gotokuji.jp/en/manekineko/).
The figurines are white glazed ceramic with a raised right paw, red collar and golden bell (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maneki_neko_by_Plus-Tech-Railways_in_Tokyo.jpg).

facts: The komaneko are stone guardian cats at Kotohira Shrine, Mineyama, Kyotango, replacing the usual komainu (https://www.kyoto-np.com/en/articles/-/825).

Kijima Shrine within the grounds, where the cats stand, was established in 1830 (Bunsei 13) by Mineyama domain chirimen merchants (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%81%93%E3%81%BE%E3%81%AD%E3%81%93%E3%81%BE%E3%81%A4%E3%82%8A).

The pair was designated a cultural property of Kyotango City in 2020 as 'Kotohira Shrine stone komaneko' (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%81%93%E3%81%BE%E3%81%AD%E3%81%93%E3%81%BE%E3%81%A4%E3%82%8A).
The left cat is the mother holding a kitten and the right the father, in 'a' and 'un' postures (https://photoguide.jp/log/2019/03/kyoto-by-the-sea-tango-peninsula-and-chirimen-silk/).

facts: Met record: design likely influenced by groupings of blue and white Dutch Delft tiles forming an image of a sitting cat (https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/13576).

rights.reason: 19th-century anonymous Thai court manuscript; creator long deceased and work predates 1930.

facts: The image is a photo of Tamra Maew Manuscript #247 held in the National Library of Thailand (Commons file TamraMaewSuphalak.jpg).
The Suphalak (Thong Daeng) is a solid reddish-brown copper-colored Thai cat variety first described in the Tamra Maew manuscripts (Wikipedia: Suphalak).
Tamra Maew manuscripts are thought to originate from the Ayutthaya Kingdom (1351–1767); surviving examples date from the 19th century (Wikipedia: Suphalak).
Over a dozen Tamra Maew manuscripts are kept in the National Library of Thailand, with others in the British Library and National Library of Australia (Wikipedia: Suphalak).
